skills.name: Recognising narrative, descriptive, expository and argumentative texts

note.text: A narrative organises events; description creates a picture through selected detail; exposition explains a topic or process; argument advances a claim with reasons. These functions can overlap: a narrative may describe a setting, and an argument may explain background. Classify the dominant work done by the excerpt rather than spotting an isolated word and assuming the whole text has one pure form.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to identify a dominant text function and recognise mixed features. Builds on: audience and purpose. Leads to: summary and purposeful composition.

sections.heading: Understand the pattern

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original models: Bih opened the hall, then discovered the missing key — narrative sequence. Dust lay along the narrow window ledge — description. A loan record links a borrower to an item — explanation. The club should retain loan records because they make returns traceable — argument. The same subject can support different text purposes.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Ask what the passage mainly does: recount events, depict, explain or argue. Support the choice with a structural feature. A first-person pronoun alone does not determine the type.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve the intended meaning and form.
example: A narrative can never include a description. Correction: Events can be developed alongside setting or character detail.
Description must list every visible object. Correction: Details are selected to create a relevant impression.
Any explanation automatically argues for a disputed policy. Correction: Explanation can clarify without advocating a policy.
An unsupported opinion and a developed argument are identical. Correction: Argument needs reasons and an intelligible relation to its claim.

pick.q: Original excerpt: A request enters the register, the organiser checks availability, and a reply confirms the booking. Its main function is to explain the process. Which category fits?
w: Argumentative solely because it has verbs
Descriptive solely because it names an organiser
A poem proved by the commas
e: Verbs occur in many text types.
Naming a person does not establish description as dominant.
Punctuation does not prove verse.
pick.y: The stated dominant function is process explanation.

pick.q: Original excerpt: The hall should stay open later because many pupils arrive after chores. Which dominant function is supported?
w: Only a list with no claim
A narrative solely because pupils are mentioned
e: It advocates a policy with a reason.
Should and because connect claim and reason.
Mentioning people does not establish an event sequence.
pick.y: Identify the proposal and its support.

pick.q: Original excerpt: The pale walls enclosed a cool, echoing room. The dominant function is what?
w: A complete sequence of several events
e: No policy claim is advanced.
The line presents qualities rather than a sequence.
No quantities or calculations appear.
pick.y: Selected sensory qualities build an impression.
